blocks.text: Your sensitive information may already be out there. Here are the notable data breaches in the country.

What happens when a stranger knows your name, home, accounts, and passwords? To some, a data breach just shows an institution’s security vulnerabilities. But the more information about you is leaked into the black market, the more you put yourself at risk of attacks.

Data breaches refer to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure, or access to sensitive information. This includes personal and financial information. Once threat actors gain access, they can weaponize it to steal time, money, and peace of mind or sell it to other threat actors for financial gain.

Breaches may happen when an employee loses confidential information that can be accessed by the public or shares it with the wrong person, wants to ruin the company’s reputation, or does so for personal profit. Hackers can also cause data breaches to steal data. They may act independently or as part of an organized group.
How leaked data pieces assemble your digital identity

A single leaked detail might seem harmless. But once collated, it puts you at risk. Tap the data categories below to see how cybercriminals piece together stolen records—and how each piece escalates your real-world risk.

Select any piece of personal data above to see what bad actors can do with that specific combination of leaked information.

Once they have this information, they can sell it on the black market or to threat actors. Attackers can use the data to make personalized attacks, scams, unauthorized transactions, or identity theft.

The Data Privacy Act of 2012 requires Personal Information Controllers (PICs)—which include both government agencies and private institutions— to notify the National Privacy Commission (NPC) and affected data subjects with a detailed report. This includes the nature of the breach, the pieces of information exposed, and measures they will take to address it.

This report should be given within 72 hours from the time they identified or have reasonable belief that a breach has occurred. This prompts an investigation by the commission and allows data subjects to launch remedial measures to prevent another data breach.
These PICs and their respective Data Protection Officers (DPOs) are accountable for adhering to the law. They are also not allowed to conceal these types of security breaches.
